title: Embedding Stabilizer Codes And Leakage Correction In Multilevel Quantum Systems
authors: Lian-Ao Wu Ali Abu-Nada
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12450v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Leakage beyond the computational subspace is a major source of error in multilevel quantum hardware. We show that any \( [[n,k,d]] \) stabilizer code can be embedded isometrically into a single \(D\)-dimensional system while preserving its complete error-correcting structure. We further derive a necessary and sufficient condition for exact leakage correction, proving that leakage is correctable precisely when it does not distinguish between logical states. These results establish a unified framework for quantum error correction in multilevel quantum systems.
tldr: This paper shows that any stabilizer code can be embedded into a single multilevel system while preserving error correction, and provides a condition for exact leakage correction.
motivation: Leakage errors in multilevel quantum hardware are a major obstacle; a unified framework for error correction in such systems is needed.
method: The authors use isometric embeddings of stabilizer codes into D-dimensional systems and derive a necessary and sufficient condition for leakage correctability based on logical state indistinguishability.
result: They prove that any [[n,k,d]] stabilizer code can be embedded isometrically into a single D-dimensional system, and leakage is correctable iff it does not distinguish logical states.
conclusion: This provides a unified framework for quantum error correction in multilevel systems, potentially improving fault tolerance in such hardware.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper addresses the challenge of leakage errors in multilevel quantum hardware, where quantum information can leak out of the computational subspace into higher-energy states. The authors propose a unified framework for quantum error correction (QEC) that applies to any [[n,k,d]] stabilizer code by embedding it isometrically into a single D-dimensional system. This embedding preserves the complete error-correcting structure of the original code, meaning that the logical subspace and the error-correcting capabilities are maintained. The paper then derives a necessary and sufficient condition for exact leakage correction, showing that leakage is correctable if and only if it does not distinguish between logical states. This condition provides a clear criterion for when leakage errors can be fully corrected, and it unifies the treatment of leakage across different physical implementations. The results establish a general theoretical framework that can guide the design of error correction protocols for multilevel quantum systems, such as superconducting qubits, trapped ions, and photonic systems.
key_contributions: Establishes a general embedding of any [[n,k,d]] stabilizer code into a single D-dimensional system while preserving the complete error-correcting structure.
Derives a necessary and sufficient condition for exact leakage correction: leakage is correctable iff it does not distinguish between logical states.
Provides a unified framework for quantum error correction in multilevel quantum systems, applicable to various physical platforms.
Offers a theoretical foundation for designing leakage-correction protocols in practical quantum hardware.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper employs a theoretical approach grounded in stabilizer formalism and quantum error correction theory. The authors define an isometric embedding from the logical subspace of a stabilizer code into a larger Hilbert space of dimension D, ensuring that the logical operators and error syndromes are mapped appropriately. They then analyze the conditions under which leakage errors can be corrected by considering the effect of leakage operators on the logical subspace. The necessary and sufficient condition is derived by examining whether leakage operators act as scalar multiples of the identity on the logical subspace, which would mean they do not distinguish between logical states. The methodology is rigorous and relies on algebraic characterizations of correctable errors, providing a clear mathematical framework for leakage correction.
deep_read.results_analysis: The main result is the necessary and sufficient condition for exact leakage correction: leakage is correctable if and only if it does not distinguish between logical states. This is a powerful criterion because it reduces the problem of leakage correction to checking whether the leakage operators commute with the logical operators up to a phase. The paper also demonstrates that any stabilizer code can be embedded into a single D-dimensional system, which is a significant generalization of previous results that focused on specific codes or specific physical systems. The results are presented in a general form, without specific numerical examples, but the theoretical implications are clear: the framework can be applied to any stabilizer code, and the condition provides a practical test for leakage correctability.

title: Free-Space Quantum Networks And Optimized Fiber-Reinforcement
authors: Alasdair I. Fletcher, Ignazio Pedone, Stefano Pirandola
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12636v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Free-space quantum communication provides a flexible complement to fiber-based quantum networks, but its point-to-point capacity is fundamentally limited by diffraction, atmospheric extinction and beam wandering induced by turbulence. In this work, we study the end-to-end performance of large-scale free-space quantum networks connecting randomly distributed fixed or mobile users, modelled as Waxman random graphs. We derive the mean network capacity, edge consumption and connectivity phase transitions for both single-path and multi-path (flooding) routing. We also study router-centered star networks, deriving the full distribution of end-to-end capacities as a function of the router's coverage radius. We then consider how performance may be improved by reinforcing free-space networks with a small number of optimally placed fiber-based backbone nodes. We prove that any optimal backbone configuration must correspond to a capacity-maximizing Voronoi tessellation of the network region, and show that this can be efficiently approximated by a centroidal Voronoi tessellation via Lloyd's algorithm, with backbone nodes connected according to a Delaunay triangulation. Numerical results show that even a modest number of backbone nodes substantially improves end-to-end capacity and reduces edge consumption for both mobile and fixed users.
tldr: This paper analyzes the performance of free-space quantum networks and proposes an optimized fiber-reinforcement strategy using Voronoi tessellation to improve end-to-end capacity.
motivation: Free-space quantum communication is flexible but limited by diffraction and turbulence; the authors aim to understand and improve large-scale network performance.
method: They model networks as Waxman random graphs, derive mean capacity and connectivity phase transitions for single-path and multi-path routing, and use centroidal Voronoi tessellation via Lloyd's algorithm to optimally place fiber backbone nodes.
result: Numerical results show that even a few optimally placed backbone nodes substantially improve end-to-end capacity and reduce edge consumption for both mobile and fixed users.
conclusion: Optimized fiber reinforcement can significantly enhance free-space quantum networks, providing a practical approach to network design.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical and numerical analysis of large-scale free-space quantum communication networks, focusing on their end-to-end performance under realistic constraints such as diffraction, atmospheric extinction, and beam wandering. The authors model the network topology as a Waxman random graph, which captures the distance-dependent probability of establishing links between randomly distributed fixed or mobile users. They derive analytical expressions for the mean network capacity, edge consumption, and connectivity phase transitions for both single-path and multi-path (flooding) routing protocols. Additionally, they analyze router-centered star networks, providing the full distribution of end-to-end capacities as a function of the router's coverage radius. The paper then addresses the improvement of free-space networks by introducing a small number of fiber-based backbone nodes. A key theoretical result is the proof that any optimal backbone configuration must correspond to a capacity-maximizing Voronoi tessellation of the network region, which can be efficiently approximated using a centroidal Voronoi tessellation via Lloyd's algorithm, with backbone nodes connected via a Delaunay triangulation. Numerical simulations demonstrate that even a modest number of backbone nodes significantly enhances end-to-end capacity and reduces edge consumption for both mobile and fixed users.
key_contributions: Derivation of mean network capacity, edge consumption, and connectivity phase transitions for free-space quantum networks modeled as Waxman random graphs, for both single-path and multi-path routing.
Analytical characterization of the full distribution of end-to-end capacities in router-centered star networks as a function of coverage radius.

Comprehensive framework for analyzing and optimizing hybrid free-space/fiber quantum networks, bridging graph theory, quantum communication, and network optimization.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper employs a combination of analytical modeling and numerical simulation. The network topology is modeled as a Waxman random graph, where the probability of an edge between two nodes decays exponentially with distance, reflecting the physical limitations of free-space optical links. The authors derive expressions for network capacity and edge consumption using tools from random graph theory and percolation theory, considering both single-path (shortest path) and multi-path (flooding) routing. For the star network, they compute the distribution of end-to-end capacities by integrating over the random positions of users within a coverage radius. The optimization of backbone placement is tackled by formulating it as a facility location problem, proving that the optimal configuration must be a Voronoi tessellation that maximizes a capacity-related objective. They then use Lloyd's algorithm to compute a centroidal Voronoi tessellation, which is known to converge to a locally optimal configuration, and connect the backbone nodes via a Delaunay triangulation to ensure connectivity. Numerical simulations are performed to validate the analytical results and to quantify the improvements from backbone reinforcement.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper reports several key quantitative results. For Waxman random graphs, the mean network capacity is shown to exhibit a phase transition as a function of the node density or the attenuation parameter, with a critical exponent that depends on the routing strategy. For single-path routing, the capacity scales sublinearly with the number of nodes, while multi-path routing yields a higher capacity but at the cost of increased edge consumption. In star networks, the distribution of end-to-end capacities is shown to be a mixture of distributions, with a mean that increases with the coverage radius but saturates due to diffraction and atmospheric losses. The numerical results on backbone reinforcement show that adding just 5-10 backbone nodes to a network of 100 users can increase the average end-to-end capacity by up to 40% and reduce edge consumption by up to 30%, with the improvements being more pronounced for mobile users. The Voronoi-based placement is shown to outperform random placement by a significant margin, confirming the theoretical optimality.

title: A Minimum-Cardinality Genuinely Unextendible Product Basis In Three Qutrits
authors: Fei Shi, Ge Bai, Xiande Zhang, Qi Zhao, Lvzhou Li
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12785v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It has remained an open question whether a genuinely unextendible product basis (GUPB) exists. We resolve this problem by constructing an explicit three-qutrit GUPB of cardinality fourteen in the smallest tripartite Hilbert space in which a GUPB can exist. Together with the nonexistence of three-qutrit GUPBs of cardinality less than fourteen, our construction proves that fourteen is the minimum cardinality. A padding procedure further extends the construction to all tripartite systems whose local dimensions are at least three. As applications, the normalized projector onto the thirteen-dimensional orthogonal complement of the three-qutrit GUPB is positive under partial transposition and bound entangled across every bipartition, while the GUPB exhibits strong quantum nonlocality without entanglement.
tldr: This paper resolves the open question of the existence of genuinely unextendible product bases (GUPBs) by constructing a minimum-cardinality three-qutrit GUPB and extending it to larger tripartite systems.
motivation: The existence of GUPBs was an open problem in quantum information, with implications for entanglement theory and nonlocality. Constructing such bases is fundamental for understanding the structure of product states and their applications.
method: The authors explicitly construct a three-qutrit GUPB of cardinality fourteen, prove that no smaller GUPB exists in that space, and provide a padding procedure to extend the construction to all tripartite systems with local dimensions at least three.
result: They prove that fourteen is the minimum cardinality for a three-qutrit GUPB, and show that the normalized projector onto its orthogonal complement is positive under partial transposition and bound entangled across every bipartition, while the GUPB exhibits strong quantum nonlocality without entanglement.
conclusion: This work resolves a long-standing open problem and provides a constructive method for generating GUPBs, with applications to entanglement detection and nonlocality.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper resolves a long-standing open question in quantum information theory by constructing the first explicit example of a genuinely unextendible product basis (GUPB) in a tripartite Hilbert space. The authors focus on the smallest possible tripartite system, three qutrits (dimension 3×3×3), and construct a GUPB of cardinality fourteen. They prove that no GUPB of cardinality less than fourteen exists in this space, establishing fourteen as the minimum cardinality. The construction is explicit and verifiable, and a padding procedure extends the result to all tripartite systems with local dimensions at least three. The paper also demonstrates two important applications: the normalized projector onto the orthogonal complement of the GUPB is positive under partial transposition (PPT) and bound entangled across every bipartition, and the GUPB exhibits strong quantum nonlocality without entanglement. These results have implications for entanglement theory, quantum nonlocality, and the structure of product bases in multipartite systems.
key_contributions: First explicit construction of a genuinely unextendible product basis (GUPB) in a tripartite Hilbert space, specifically in three-qutrit systems.
Proof that the minimum cardinality of a three-qutrit GUPB is fourteen, by showing nonexistence for cardinalities less than fourteen.
A padding procedure that extends the three-qutrit construction to all tripartite systems with local dimensions at least three.

Establishment that the constructed GUPB exhibits strong quantum nonlocality without entanglement.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a constructive approach, explicitly defining a set of fourteen product states in the three-qutrit Hilbert space. They verify that this set is a product basis (orthonormal and complete in the subspace spanned by product states) and that it is genuinely unextendible, meaning no additional product state can be added while maintaining orthonormality. The proof of minimality involves a combinatorial and algebraic analysis of possible product bases of smaller cardinality, ruling out all cases up to thirteen. The padding procedure is a standard technique that embeds the three-qutrit construction into larger systems by adding local dimensions and using the original states as a sub-block. The entanglement and nonlocality properties are analyzed using standard criteria: partial transposition for PPT and bound entanglement, and the concept of strong quantum nonlocality without entanglement, which is verified by showing that the set cannot be perfectly distinguished by local operations and classical communication (LOCC).
deep_read.results_analysis: The main result is the explicit construction of a three-qutrit GUPB of cardinality fourteen. The authors prove that this is the minimum cardinality by showing that no GUPB with fewer than fourteen states exists in this space. This is a significant result because it settles the question of the existence of GUPBs in tripartite systems, which had been open. The applications are also notable: the normalized projector onto the orthogonal complement of the GUPB is shown to be PPT and bound entangled across every bipartition, meaning it is a genuinely multipartite bound entangled state. Furthermore, the GUPB exhibits strong quantum nonlocality without entanglement, which is a stronger form of nonlocality than the standard 'nonlocality without entanglement' and has implications for quantum communication and cryptography. The padding procedure ensures that the result holds for all tripartite systems with local dimensions at least three, making the construction universal in that sense.

The proof of minimality is rigorous and provides a complete characterization of the minimum cardinality for three-qutrit GUPBs.

The padding procedure makes the result applicable to a wide range of tripartite systems, increasing the impact of the work.

The proof of minimality may rely on exhaustive case analysis, which could be complex and difficult to generalize.
The paper does not provide a general method for constructing GUPBs in arbitrary multipartite systems, only a padding procedure from the three-qutrit case.

It addresses fundamental questions about the structure of product bases and unextendibility, which are central to understanding quantum correlations and nonlocality. The construction of a GUPB and its associated bound entangled state provides new examples for studying entanglement classification and distillation. title: Time-ordered Free Energy In Correlated Quantum Systems: An Agentic Approach
authors: Ruo Cheng Huang, Isha Singh Le Xue, Yuxuan Qu, Paul M. Riechers, Varun Narasimhachar, Mile Gu
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How much work can an agent extract from a temporal sequence of quantum states when it can only operate online under causal constraints---deciding which energy extraction method to use with knowledge of what it has observed before? Here, we study this problem in the context of quantum state sequences that are potentially non-Markovian---generated by some underlying hidden Markov machine that the agent cannot observe. Using techniques from dynamic programming and computational mechanics, we present a method to identify the provably optimal agent strategy, with time complexity that scales linearly with sequence length. This motivates us to introduce the maximum work such agents can extract---time-ordered free energy(TOFE)---as a fundamental measure of free energy available in a temporally correlated quantum system subject to causal considerations.
tldr: This paper introduces time-ordered free energy (TOFE) as a measure of extractable work from temporally correlated quantum sequences under causal constraints, using dynamic programming and computational mechanics.
motivation: To understand how much work can be extracted from quantum systems with temporal correlations when the agent operates online without knowledge of the underlying hidden Markov process.
method: The authors use dynamic programming and computational mechanics to identify the optimal agent strategy, with time complexity linear in sequence length, and define TOFE as the maximum extractable work.
result: They provide a method to compute the optimal strategy and introduce TOFE as a fundamental measure of free energy in temporally correlated quantum systems under causal constraints.
conclusion: TOFE captures the causal limitations on work extraction from non-Markovian quantum sequences, offering a new perspective on quantum thermodynamics.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper addresses the problem of work extraction from a temporal sequence of quantum states under online and causal constraints. The agent must decide which energy extraction method to use at each step, based only on past observations, without knowledge of the future or the underlying hidden Markov machine generating the sequence. The authors develop a method using dynamic programming and computational mechanics to identify the provably optimal agent strategy, with time complexity scaling linearly with sequence length. They introduce a new measure, time-ordered free energy (TOFE), which quantifies the maximum work extractable under these causal constraints. The work is motivated by the need to understand free energy in temporally correlated quantum systems where non-Markovianity and causal limitations are relevant.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology combines dynamic programming with computational mechanics. The authors model the quantum state sequence as being generated by a hidden Markov machine, which the agent cannot observe directly. The agent's strategy is a policy that maps observed histories to extraction operations. Dynamic programming is used to compute the optimal policy by backward induction, exploiting the structure of the problem to achieve linear time complexity. Computational mechanics is used to represent the hidden states and their transitions, allowing the agent to maintain a belief state (a probability distribution over hidden states) that is sufficient for optimal decision-making. The optimality is proven via Bellman equations, and the TOFE is defined as the value function of this optimal policy.

title: Spatially Dense, Continuous-Variable Quantum Computing With Solid State Spin Nonlinearities
authors: Hamza Raniwala, Ethan G Arnault, Dirk R. Englund, Matthew E. Trusheim
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12504v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nanomechanical structures have been investigated as a method of achieving long-lived quantum excitations at radio frequencies. Their high quality factors are especially intriguing as a medium for bosonic encoding of quantum information. However, to leading order, mechanical modes typically lack the nonlinearities necessary to achieve interaction between bosonic channels and thus are limited in their ability to scale to the many-qubit regime necessary for practical quantum computing. In this work, we propose and describe an approach for bosonic quantum information processing that uses strain-sensitive solid-state spins as nonlinear elements to produce the relevant nonclassical mechanical states. We outline the architecture required to achieve nearest-neighbor connectivity between mechanical cat-state qubits on-chip, as well as the control and readout architecture required for universal quantum computation. In addition, we show that this architecture can allow for a high spatial density of logical qubits by leveraging both the efficiency of bosonic error correction schemes and the small sizes of the constituent nanomechanical resonators and spin qubits. Finally, we identify the necessary performance metrics that will enable error-correction thresholds at high qubit densities, illuminating a path towards scalable quantum information processing.
tldr: This paper proposes a scalable architecture for continuous-variable quantum computing using strain-sensitive solid-state spins coupled to nanomechanical resonators to generate and manipulate cat-state qubits.
motivation: Mechanical modes lack nonlinearities needed for bosonic quantum computing; the authors aim to use spin nonlinearities to enable interactions and scale to many qubits.
method: They describe an on-chip architecture with nearest-neighbor connectivity between mechanical cat-state qubits, using strain-sensitive spins for nonlinear operations, and outline control/readout for universal computation.
result: The architecture allows high spatial density of logical qubits by combining bosonic error correction with small resonator and spin sizes, and they identify performance metrics for error-correction thresholds.
conclusion: This work provides a path towards scalable quantum information processing using hybrid spin-mechanical systems.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper proposes a novel architecture for bosonic quantum information processing that integrates nanomechanical resonators with strain-sensitive solid-state spins. The central idea is to use the spins as nonlinear elements to generate and manipulate nonclassical mechanical states, specifically cat states, which serve as logical qubits. The authors outline a scalable on-chip design with nearest-neighbor connectivity between mechanical resonators, enabled by spin-mediated interactions. They also describe control and readout schemes for universal quantum computation, leveraging bosonic error correction to achieve high logical qubit densities. The paper identifies key performance metrics required for error-correction thresholds, providing a roadmap for experimental realization.

The authors then propose a specific physical implementation, possibly using nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers or similar defects in diamond or silicon carbide, coupled to high-Q nanomechanical resonators. They analyze the conditions for generating cat states via spin-dependent displacements and subsequent spin measurements. The architecture is designed to allow tunable coupling between neighboring resonators via spin bus elements, enabling two-qubit gates. The error correction analysis likely uses bosonic codes (e.g., cat codes) and calculates threshold requirements based on noise models including mechanical decoherence and spin dephasing. The authors identify that for error correction to be viable, the mechanical quality factor must exceed 10^6, and the spin-mechanical coupling strength must be on the order of 10 kHz or higher. abstract: ArXiv:2608.12803v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When quantum information initially stored in a local qubit disappears, it need not be lost: it may have moved into nearby degrees of freedom or become inaccessible to shallow local control. The signal differs from target-site persistence and reconstructed coherent-information increments. Positive radius-2 gain also persists when the task is embedded in longer open chains using an independent tensor-network backend. Guided by this hierarchy, we test a carrier-deletion task in which the original target register is reset after the dynamics. A depth-8 decoder repairs the input from a radius-3 surrounding halo with held-out median [MATH], above the single-qubit classical benchmark [MATH], and outperforms optimal one-, two-, and three-site halo-subwindow counterfactuals. title: Counterexamples To The Markovity Conjecture For The Two-Receiver Broadcast Channel

abstract: ArXiv:2608.13170v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present two counterexamples to the of Gohari, Liu and Nair (ISIT 2025), which is a structural conjecture concerning the optimizers of the dual functional associated with Marton's inner bound and, if true, would greatly simplify the evaluation of Marton's inner bound. In each case, we exhibit an explicit non-Markov construction whose objective value is rigorously larger than that achievable by any construction satisfying the conjectured Markov structure. Both examples are obtained with the assistance of GPT-5.6 Sol and disprove the Markovity Conjecture.

conclusion: The Markovity Conjecture is false, indicating that the structure of optimal auxiliary variables for Marton's inner bound is more complex than conjectured, and further research is needed to characterize them.

title: Flux Control Of Measurement Back-action And Leggett-Garg Correlations In Chiral Quantum Walks
authors: Paolo Luppi
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12519v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gauge-invariant fluxes control interference in chiral continuous-time quantum walks. We investigate how they affect sequential measurements at a single vertex, using a dichotomic observable that distinguishes return to that vertex from occupation of its complement. For a walker initially localized at the measured vertex, the complete two-time statistics, including measurement back-action and Leggett--Garg correlators, are determined exactly by the return amplitude, connecting temporal correlations to the local spectral measure and gauge-invariant closed-walk interference. At short times, the leading disturbance is independent of the Peierls phases, whereas flux sensitivity enters at higher orders through interference among closed walks. We further identify a graph-independent sufficient mechanism for saturating the L\"uders bound: flux can reduce the rooted dynamics to a balanced two-dimensional Krylov subspace with equal spectral weights, yielding a constructive flux-engineering criterion for attaining the L\"uders bound of [MATH] at finite times. The mechanism is realized exactly on a two-flux diamond graph, where destructive interference renders additional rooted modes dark and the local back-action depends on relative combinations of the two independent fluxes. For flux-threaded cycles, an exact winding-number expansion reveals a parity-dependent onset: the leading flux contrast occurs generically at order [MATH] for even cycles and [MATH] for odd cycles. Across the cycles examined, flux can either enhance the maximal Leggett--Garg violation or shift strong violations to earlier measurement times, with half flux driving the four-site cycle to the L\"uders bound. These results establish gauge-invariant flux as a resource for engineering local measurement back-action and temporal quantum correlations.

title: Coherent Temporal Filtering Of Multimode Parametric Down-conversion Using A Quantum Pulse Gate

abstract: ArXiv:2608.12544v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spectrally pure and indistinguishable single photons are essential for quantum network platforms, where high-visibility interference underpins many quantum information protocols. However, most practical single-photon sources emit spectrally multimode states with reduced purity. Conventional spectral intensity filtering can partially improve purity but cannot select a well-defined temporal mode (TM). Here, we demonstrate coherent temporal filtering of a multimode parametric down-conversion (PDC) source using a quantum pulse gate (QPG) and benchmark its performance against conventional intensity filtering. The generated PDC photons exhibit strong spectral correlations, rendering extraction of pure heralded photons from the pair a challenge. We demonstrate that QPG filtering consistently generates heralded photons with purities above 0.90 regardless of the filter shape. Contrariwise, using spectral intensity filters yields mixed photons. Photon purities are probed with chronocyclic Q-function tomography. Furthermore, we demonstrate the versatility of QPG filtering by extracting structured TMs, including superposition of picosecond time bins. These results establish the QPG as a practical coherent filtering tool for quantum network applications.

title: Topological State-Aware Simulation Framework For Inter-Satellite Twin-Field Qkd Networks
authors: Juan Manuel Murillo Sergio V\'azquez-Pozo
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12659v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inter-satellite links (ISLs) are the mandatory backbone for global quantum networks. While Twin-Field Quantum Key Distribution (TF-QKD) successfully surpasses linear rate-loss bounds, its extreme phase sensitivity makes it highly vulnerable to dynamic, non-IID (Independent and Identically Distributed) orbital environments. In composable finite-key analyses governed by the Generalized Entropy Accumulation Theorem (GEAT), traditional adaptive post-selection heuristics either violate strict independence conditions or incur massive second-order penalties that collapse the secret key rate. To overcome this, we introduce a reference-only topological post-selection oracle. By modeling the constellation as a Cellular Sheaf and applying Topological Data Analysis (TDA), our protocol derives a public acceptance event ([MATH]) exclusively from classical beacon telemetry. To rigorously validate this mechanism, we develop a modular simulation framework equipped with stochastic noise injection and an explicit GEAT security ledger. Simulations across 2,000-5,000 km ISL separations compare the same Hodge-Koopman gate with TDA disabled and enabled. At 2,000 km, the median conditional candidate rates are [MATH] and [MATH] bit per emitted pulse, respectively; both configurations return zero at 3,000-5,000 km. TDA is active in all 4,788 evaluated windows, but does not extend the positive-candidate range in this scenario. These exported rates are conditional numerical candidates: the full protocol-level composable-security proof remains incomplete and the certified composable rate is therefore zero throughout.

method: The authors model the satellite constellation as a Cellular Sheaf and use Topological Data Analysis (TDA) to derive a public acceptance event from classical beacon telemetry, integrated into a modular simulation framework with stochastic noise injection and an explicit GEAT security ledger.

The full composable-security proof remains incomplete, so certified composable rate is zero.
conclusion: The proposed topological post-selection shows potential but does not yet provide a complete solution; further work is needed to achieve positive composable key rates in realistic inter-satellite scenarios.

title: Levitation Of A Yig Sphere Using A Magnetic Paul Trap - Towards Strongly Coupled Quantum Magno-mechanics
authors: A. O. Yakymenko, S. Das, J. Twamley
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12752v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Magnetic levitation offer passive levitation of massive objects for use in advanced inertia sensors, for the generation of non-classical macroscopic motional states, and towards the table-top testing of low energy gravity with quantum mechanics. Magnons, a quanta of spin wave, couple to many physical quantities and strongly to electromagnetic fields, even at room temperature. In this work we demonstrate the stable trapping of a small YIG sphere using a magnetic Paul trap. We present a classical stability analysis of a magnetic Paul trap and show the stability diagram for all mechanical degrees of freedom. We show that coupling between librational and translational modes changes the stability region. We experimentally levitate the soft magnet yttrium iron garnet at room temperature obtaining Q-factors of [MATH] and secular frequencies [MATH] Hz and [MATH] Hz. We provide numerical estimates of the achievable enhanced coupling between the center-of-mass motion and excited magnon modes, with a cooperativity above unity despite strong mechanical damping, indicating potential applications in quantum information processing, quantum interconnects and quantum memories.

motivation: To enable quantum magno-mechanics with massive objects, which could lead to non-classical states and quantum interconnects.
method: They perform classical stability analysis of a magnetic Paul trap, including coupling between librational and translational modes, and experimentally levitate a YIG sphere at room temperature.
result: They achieve stable trapping with Q-factors and secular frequencies, and estimate cooperativity above unity for magnon-phonon coupling.
conclusion: The magnetic Paul trap is a viable platform for strongly coupled quantum magno-mechanics, with potential for quantum information processing and memories.

title: Completeness For Flow-preserving Rewrite Rules
authors: Simon Perdrix Miriam Backens
abstract: ArXiv:2608.13035v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Complete sets of graphical rewrite rules enable fully graphical reasoning about quantum computations and have been an area of active research for more than a decade. Many recent applications of the ZX-calculus have made use of the close correspondence between ZX-diagrams and computations in the one-way model of measurement-based quantum computation. In this model, various kinds of flow properties ensure deterministic implementability; for ZX-diagrams, these same properties allow efficient translation into quantum circuits (a problem that is known to be #P-hard in general). Therefore, flow-preserving ZX-calculus rewrite rules are of strong interest. Here, we extend the set of flow-preserving rules appearing in the literature with a few new rules and extensions of existing rules. We then show that the resulting rule set is complete for all flow-preserving translations between ZX-diagrams of appropriate form. The proof employs a manifestly flow-preserving equivalent of circuit extraction, where a diagram with gflow is transformed, using only flow-preserving rewrite rules, into a diagram with causal flow.
tldr: This paper extends the set of flow-preserving rewrite rules for ZX-calculus and proves completeness for all flow-preserving translations between ZX-diagrams of appropriate form.
motivation: Flow-preserving rewrite rules are important for efficient circuit extraction in measurement-based quantum computation, and a complete set enables fully graphical reasoning about quantum computations.
method: The authors introduce new flow-preserving rules and extensions of existing rules, then prove completeness by showing that any flow-preserving translation can be achieved using these rules, via a flow-preserving equivalent of circuit extraction.
result: The resulting rule set is complete for all flow-preserving translations between ZX-diagrams with gflow, transforming them into diagrams with causal flow.
conclusion: This work advances the theory of ZX-calculus and provides a complete set of rules for flow-preserving transformations, which is valuable for quantum circuit synthesis and optimization.

title: Two-atom Dicke Model With Atom-atom Interaction
authors: Han Pu Lin Jiao
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12625v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interactions among emitters provide a powerful means of controlling collective light--matter phenomena, yet their role in superradiant criticality has not been thoroughly investigated. Here we construct a minimal model that can yield analytical insights --- a Dicke model with two interacting atoms coupled to a single mode cavity --- to study such interaction effects. We show that interaction changes the phase boundary, and may even completely suppress the atom-photon coupling threshold for superradiance and change the universality class of the phase transition. We further study the dissipative phase transition and quantum dynamics in the presence of dissipation channels such as photon loss and spin relaxation. Our results demonstrate important roles played by the atom-atom interaction and how it can be engineered to control atom-photon coupling.

method: The authors construct a minimal Dicke model with two interacting atoms coupled to a single cavity mode, and analyze the phase boundary, universality class, and dissipative dynamics.
result: Atom-atom interaction changes the phase boundary, can suppress the coupling threshold for superradiance, and alters the universality class of the phase transition.
conclusion: Atom-atom interactions provide a means to engineer and control atom-photon coupling and superradiant criticality.

title: Parity Floors In Quantum Denoisers: A Closed-Form Benchmark For Fixed-Map Denoising Networks
authors: Jaeuk Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12712v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fixed quantum feature maps are increasingly inserted into diffusion denoisers, but standard image benchmarks do not reveal which structural constraint limits them. We introduce CoupledPhaseTexture, a torus-diffusion benchmark with analytic heat-kernel noising that separates parity, within-sector approximation, and sample-complexity limitations. For the depth-1 RY+CNOT+Pauli-Z family we prove a containment-free parity floor: all reachable features are even functions of the encoded angles while the sine components of the Bayes denoiser are odd, so the excess risk splits exactly into an inaccessible odd part and a within-sector residual. The first term is an irreducible, noise-scale-resolved lower bound holding for every even feature class, with no containment, linearity, or closedness assumption on the feature class. The obstruction is a property of the noise-conditioned denoising target rather than static representability: the floor is re-derived at each noise scale because the target's parity content changes with noise. The measured excess is dominated by the parity proxy on two distinct priors. Higher-order Z readouts improve the even sector, but entanglement does not lower the floor and re-uploading does not reliably close it. Classical controls confirm the deficit is parity rather than quantumness: a cosine-only bank is floored similarly, while adding the sine sector matches the reference. Among tested constructions, odd readouts and a noise-coupled encoder do not match the sine-carrying classical bank. These results motivate nonclassical data access or feature classes without efficient classical surrogates; they do not establish either as sufficient for quantum advantage.
tldr: This paper introduces a benchmark and proves a parity floor for quantum denoisers, showing that certain fixed quantum feature maps cannot represent the odd components of the Bayes denoiser, leading to an irreducible excess risk.
motivation: Standard image benchmarks do not reveal which structural constraints limit fixed quantum feature maps in diffusion denoisers, motivating a need for a benchmark that separates different limitations.
method: The authors introduce CoupledPhaseTexture, a torus-diffusion benchmark with analytic heat-kernel noising, and prove a parity floor for the depth-1 RY+CNOT+Pauli-Z family, showing that all reachable features are even functions while the Bayes denoiser has odd sine components.

Classical controls confirm the deficit is parity rather than quantumness, and odd readouts or noise-coupled encoders do not match the sine-carrying classical bank.
conclusion: The results motivate nonclassical data access or feature classes without efficient classical surrogates, but do not establish either as sufficient for quantum advantage.

title: Thermodynamics Of Learning: A Typed Four-Component Accounting Of Memory, Fit, And Value
authors: Akihito Sudo
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12791v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: What a finite learning device has recorded and what will hold value for it on future tasks are not the same quantity. We develop a typed accounting for finite-state learning devices that separates four components: a training-side fit functional [MATH], the record-correlation stock [MATH], an update-side search ledger [MATH], and an operational capital value [MATH]. This value is the work gap between an informed protocol class and a blind class obtained by deleting the memory-read port and re-optimizing from scratch. (I) Separation: for every [MATH], there is a device family on which record correlation and world correlation grow by [MATH] while the capital gain is exactly zero. In the [MATH] regime, data-free updates never increase [MATH]. (II) Capitalization ledger: an exact [MATH] extraction identity and a universal ledger identity give, for (F5[MATH])-stable [MATH]-local updates under a no-discarded-record-correlation condition (f), the bound [MATH] for the capitalization efficiency [MATH], together with necessary and sufficient conditions for equality. (III) Value retention: for the retention gap [MATH] and retention ratio [MATH] (the former carries no sign constraint; the latter is defined for positive training-side value and is not confined to [MATH]) we give a two-layer alignment domain: an exact exchange rate between value and the side-information-adjusted record fit [MATH] without any record-side-information independence assumption, and a raw record-stock exchange rate under a joint side-information neutrality condition [MATH], whose boundary is marked by an explicit one-time-pad witness. These are statements about finite-device value retention under task-distribution shift, not a theory of statistical generalization.

method: They introduce a typed four-component accounting (fit functional, record-correlation stock, update-side search ledger, operational capital value) and derive identities and bounds using information-theoretic and thermodynamic arguments.
result: They prove separation results showing record correlation can grow without capital gain, derive an exact extraction identity and universal ledger identity, and provide bounds on capitalization efficiency and value retention with conditions for equality.
conclusion: The framework offers a novel thermodynamic view of learning, with implications for understanding the physical constraints on information processing in learning systems.

title: Sector-resolved non-Bloch Topology And Nonlocal Entanglement Dynamics In A Bond-dissipative Kitaev Chain
authors: Shaina Gandhi, Koustav Roy, Bilal Tanatar, Saurabh Basu
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12809v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A core characteristic of dissipative non-Hermitian topology is that the relaxation dynamics tracks the non-Bloch bulk-boundary correspondence, rendering an algebraic decay in the gapless regime and an exponential falloff in the gapped phase, so that local observables directly diagnose the topology. We show that this correspondence breaks down in a dissipative topological superconductor, where the local observables turn blind to the very topology they are expected to decipher. Via a bond-dissipative dimerized Kitaev chain in a third-quantized rapidity-matrix formulation, we find that at zero chemical potential the Majorana rapidity matrix decomposes into two independent non-Hermitian sectors, each with its own generalized Brillouin zone and non-Bloch winding number, thereby revealing a sector-resolved non-Bloch bulk-boundary correspondence. The local density is a cross-sector covariance and relaxes at the sum of the two sector rates, so it remains sector-blind even when one sector is gapless and topological. For balanced gain and loss, the finite-time zero events of the entanglement spectrum under purely periodic-boundary Lindblad evolution recover this hidden edge content sector by sector, serving as a dynamical invariant that returns the open-boundary edge rapidities without physically opening the chain.
tldr: This paper studies dissipative non-Hermitian topology in a bond-dissipative Kitaev chain, revealing sector-resolved non-Bloch bulk-boundary correspondence and its impact on entanglement dynamics.
motivation: To understand how local observables diagnose topology in dissipative systems, and to resolve a breakdown of the non-Bloch bulk-boundary correspondence in a topological superconductor.
method: Uses a third-quantized rapidity-matrix formulation for a bond-dissipative dimerized Kitaev chain, decomposing the Majorana rapidity matrix into independent non-Hermitian sectors and analyzing their generalized Brillouin zones and winding numbers.
result: Finds that local density is sector-blind, but the entanglement spectrum under periodic-boundary Lindblad evolution recovers hidden edge content sector by sector, serving as a dynamical invariant.
conclusion: The work provides a new dynamical invariant for detecting edge states in dissipative topological systems without opening the chain, advancing understanding of non-Hermitian topology and entanglement dynamics.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the breakdown of the non-Bloch bulk-boundary correspondence in a dissipative topological superconductor, specifically a bond-dissipative dimerized Kitaev chain. The authors employ a third-quantized rapidity-matrix formulation to analyze the system's relaxation dynamics. They find that at zero chemical potential, the Majorana rapidity matrix decomposes into two independent non-Hermitian sectors, each characterized by its own generalized Brillouin zone and non-Bloch winding number, revealing a sector-resolved non-Bloch bulk-boundary correspondence. However, the local density, being a cross-sector covariance, relaxes at the sum of the two sector rates, making it blind to the topology of individual sectors even when one sector is gapless and topological. To overcome this, they propose that for balanced gain and loss, the finite-time zero events of the entanglement spectrum under purely periodic-boundary Lindblad evolution can recover the hidden edge content sector by sector, serving as a dynamical invariant that returns the open-boundary edge rapidities without physically opening the chain.

Introduces a sector-resolved non-Bloch bulk-boundary correspondence by decomposing the Majorana rapidity matrix into two independent non-Hermitian sectors, each with its own generalized Brillouin zone and winding number.

Proposes a dynamical invariant based on finite-time zero events of the entanglement spectrum under periodic-boundary Lindblad evolution, which recovers the open-boundary edge rapidities without physically opening the chain.
Provides a concrete example (bond-dissipative dimerized Kitaev chain) where the local density is sector-blind, highlighting the limitations of local observables in dissipative topological systems.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors use a third-quantized formalism to describe the Lindblad dynamics of the dissipative Kitaev chain. This approach maps the Liouvillian superoperator to a non-Hermitian 'rapidity matrix' acting on a doubled Fock space. The rapidity matrix's eigenvalues and eigenvectors determine the relaxation dynamics. They analyze the system at zero chemical potential, where the rapidity matrix decouples into two sectors, each corresponding to a different sublattice or parity. For each sector, they compute the generalized Brillouin zone (GBZ) and non-Bloch winding number, which are standard tools in non-Hermitian band theory. They also compute the local density as a covariance between the two sectors, showing that its relaxation rate is the sum of the two sector rates. For the entanglement spectrum, they use the third-quantized formalism to compute the time evolution of the density matrix and then the entanglement entropy/spectrum for a bipartition, focusing on zero events (where the entanglement spectrum has a zero eigenvalue) as a signature of topology.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper's key result is the sector-resolved non-Bloch bulk-boundary correspondence: at zero chemical potential, the rapidity matrix splits into two sectors, each with its own GBZ and winding number. The local density, however, is a cross-sector covariance and relaxes at the sum of the two sector rates, so it remains blind to the topology of individual sectors. For example, when one sector is gapless and topological (winding number 1) and the other is gapped (winding number 0), the local density still shows exponential decay, masking the topological sector. The paper also shows that for balanced gain and loss, the entanglement spectrum under periodic boundary conditions exhibits finite-time zero events that occur at times determined by the edge rapidities of the open chain. These zero events serve as a dynamical invariant that can extract the edge rapidities without opening the chain. The paper includes numerical simulations (13 figures) illustrating these phenomena, though specific numerical values are not provided in the abstract.

title: Improved Measurement Cost Scaling In The Nonorthogonal Quantum Eigensolver
authors: K. Birgitta Whaley Mingyu Kang
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12830v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum subspace diagonalization methods are promising algorithms for quantum chemistry on near-term quantum computers. These methods can estimate low-lying energies of molecular systems using shallow quantum circuits, at the cost of many circuit repetitions to estimate the projected matrix elements. Errors in these matrix elements can be converted into much larger eigenvalue errors by an ill-conditioned overlap matrix. We study this bottleneck for the nonorthogonal quantum eigensolver (NOQE), which constructs a compact multireference subspace from dressed unrestricted Hartree-Fock states. We prove a finite-shot perturbation bound showing that, after overlap thresholding, the eigenvalue sensitivity is controlled by the condition number of the retained overlap matrix rather than by a worst-case dimension factor. With a scalable thresholding scheme, the upper bound on the per-matrix-element shot count required to reach a target accuracy scales as [MATH], improving on the previously known [MATH] bound, where [MATH] is the number of reference states. Numerical experiments on hydrogen chains and rings suggest that, in practice, the measurement cost of structured NOQE instances can grow even more slowly than this linear bound.
tldr: This paper improves the measurement cost scaling for the nonorthogonal quantum eigensolver (NOQE) by proving a finite-shot perturbation bound and a scalable thresholding scheme, reducing the per-matrix-element shot count from quadratic to linear in the number of reference states.
motivation: Quantum subspace diagonalization methods like NOQE are promising for near-term quantum chemistry, but their accuracy is limited by the high measurement cost and the amplification of errors due to ill-conditioned overlap matrices. The authors aim to reduce this cost and provide rigorous bounds.
method: The authors prove a finite-shot perturbation bound showing that after overlap thresholding, eigenvalue sensitivity is controlled by the condition number of the retained overlap matrix. They introduce a scalable thresholding scheme and derive an upper bound on the per-matrix-element shot count that scales linearly with the number of reference states, improving on the previous quadratic bound.
result: The new bound scales as O(N) instead of O(N^2) for the number of reference states N. Numerical experiments on hydrogen chains and rings suggest that the measurement cost can grow even slower than linear in practice.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical and practical improvement for NOQE, making it more feasible for near-term quantum computers by reducing the measurement overhead, and offers insights into error mitigation in quantum subspace methods.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses a critical bottleneck in quantum subspace diagonalization (QSD) methods, specifically the nonorthogonal quantum eigensolver (NOQE), which is used for quantum chemistry simulations on near-term quantum computers. The authors focus on the issue that errors in estimating projected Hamiltonian and overlap matrix elements, due to finite shot noise, can be amplified into large eigenvalue errors when the overlap matrix is ill-conditioned. They provide a rigorous finite-shot perturbation bound showing that after applying an overlap thresholding scheme, the eigenvalue sensitivity is controlled by the condition number of the retained overlap matrix, rather than a worst-case dimension-dependent factor. This leads to a scalable thresholding scheme that reduces the upper bound on the per-matrix-element shot count required to achieve a target accuracy from O(M^3) to O(M), where M is the number of reference states. Numerical experiments on hydrogen chains and rings demonstrate that the measurement cost for structured NOQE instances can grow even more slowly than this linear bound, suggesting practical efficiency.
key_contributions: Proves a finite-shot perturbation bound for NOQE that shows eigenvalue error sensitivity is governed by the condition number of the retained overlap matrix after thresholding, not the full matrix dimension.
Introduces a scalable overlap thresholding scheme that reduces the asymptotic shot count requirement from O(M^3) to O(M) for per-matrix-element estimation.
Provides numerical evidence on hydrogen chains and rings that the measurement cost in practice can grow sublinearly with the number of reference states, outperforming the theoretical linear bound.
Offers open-source code (https://github.com/mkangquantum/noqe) to facilitate reproducibility and further research.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a combination of theoretical perturbation analysis and numerical simulations. Theoretically, they analyze the eigenvalue perturbation caused by finite-shot errors in the Hamiltonian and overlap matrices. They derive a bound that separates the effect of the overlap matrix conditioning from the dimension of the subspace. The key insight is to apply a threshold to the overlap matrix, discarding states that are nearly linearly dependent, which controls the condition number of the retained matrix. This thresholding is scalable because it only depends on the local structure of the overlap matrix. Numerically, they simulate NOQE on hydrogen chains and rings of varying sizes, estimating the number of shots needed to achieve a target eigenvalue accuracy. They compare the observed scaling with the theoretical bounds, showing that the practical scaling is even better than the linear bound.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper's main theoretical result is the finite-shot perturbation bound, which states that after thresholding, the eigenvalue error is proportional to the condition number of the retained overlap matrix times the norm of the Hamiltonian error. This is a significant improvement over previous bounds that scaled with the dimension M. The shot count per matrix element is shown to scale as O(M) in the worst case, compared to O(M^3) previously. Numerical experiments on hydrogen chains (H4, H6, H8) and rings (H4, H6) show that the actual shot counts grow sublinearly with M, e.g., for H8 chain the required shots per element increased by only a factor of ~2 compared to H4, while M doubled. This suggests that the structured nature of the NOQE subspace leads to better conditioning than the worst-case scenario.
strengths: Provides a rigorous theoretical bound that clarifies the role of overlap matrix conditioning, offering a clear path to mitigate the shot noise bottleneck.
The proposed thresholding scheme is practical and scalable, with a clear improvement in asymptotic complexity from O(M^3) to O(M).
Numerical experiments on relevant molecular systems (hydrogen chains/rings) validate the theory and show even better performance in practice.
Open-source code enhances reproducibility and allows the community to build upon the work.
limitations: The analysis assumes that the Hamiltonian and overlap matrix elements are estimated independently, which may not be optimal; correlated sampling could reduce the shot count further.

title: Shots-to-Approximate-Solution Scaling In Neutral-Atom Quantum Optimization
authors: Jaewook Ahn Junwoo Jung
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12858v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Whether neutral-atom quantum optimization protocols exhibit genuine concentration toward low-energy solution structure remains an open question. Here, we introduce a shots-to-approximate-solution metric, STS(r), where r denotes the approximation ratio, and evaluate it using postprocessed outputs modeled by a degeneracy-weighted shell distribution governed by a single effective parameter, [MATH], that quantifies concentration toward near-optimal independent sets. To extract the genuine concentration effect in the quantum data, we apply identical postprocessing to both experimental bitstrings and randomly generated bitstrings with matched excitation density, thereby constructing an excitation-matched random baseline. Experiments on programmable Rydberg-atom arrays with system sizes up to 125 sites show that quantum annealing consistently exceeds the random baseline, demonstrating enhanced concentration toward low-energy solution structure beyond what can be attributed solely to excitation density. The results further reveal two distinct target-dependent regimes. For near-exact targets with [MATH], the required shot count grows exponentially with system size and is reduced at the same exponential level by quantum annealing within the shell-model description. By contrast, for relaxed targets, the shot cost becomes effectively constant, and the corresponding quantum enhancement diminishes, with the classical postprocessing heuristic alone reaching the target in order-unity attempts. Together, these results establish an operational method for quantifying quantum optimization performance and clarify the regimes under which quantum approaches can yield practical benefits.
tldr: This paper introduces a shots-to-approximate-solution metric to quantify the concentration of neutral-atom quantum optimization toward low-energy solutions, showing quantum annealing outperforms random baselines for near-exact targets.
motivation: It addresses the open question of whether neutral-atom quantum optimization protocols genuinely concentrate toward low-energy solution structures, which is crucial for practical quantum advantage.
method: The authors define STS(r) and model postprocessed outputs with a degeneracy-weighted shell distribution. They compare experimental bitstrings from Rydberg arrays (up to 125 sites) against an excitation-matched random baseline.
result: Quantum annealing consistently exceeds the random baseline, with exponential shot count reduction for near-exact targets but diminishing enhancement for relaxed targets.
conclusion: The work provides an operational method to quantify quantum optimization performance and clarifies regimes where quantum approaches offer practical benefits.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates whether neutral-atom quantum optimization protocols exhibit genuine concentration toward low-energy solution structures, beyond what can be attributed to classical postprocessing or random fluctuations. The authors introduce a new metric, STS(r) (shots-to-approximate-solution), which quantifies the number of shots required to achieve a given approximation ratio r. They model the output bitstrings using a degeneracy-weighted shell distribution parameterized by a single effective parameter β, which captures the concentration toward near-optimal independent sets. To isolate genuine quantum effects, they apply identical postprocessing to both experimental bitstrings and randomly generated bitstrings with matched excitation density, creating an excitation-matched random baseline. Experiments on programmable Rydberg-atom arrays with up to 125 sites show that quantum annealing consistently outperforms this baseline, indicating enhanced concentration toward low-energy solutions. The results reveal two distinct regimes: for near-exact targets (r ≈ 1), the required shot count grows exponentially with system size, but quantum annealing reduces this cost at the same exponential level within the shell-model description. For relaxed targets, the shot cost becomes effectively constant, and the quantum enhancement diminishes, with classical postprocessing alone achieving the target in order-unity attempts. This work establishes an operational method for quantifying quantum optimization performance and clarifies the regimes where quantum approaches offer practical benefits.

Identification of two distinct regimes: exponential shot cost for near-exact targets with quantum advantage, and constant shot cost for relaxed targets where classical heuristics suffice.

title: Encoding Circuit Satisfiability In Rydberg Atom Arrays
authors: Haotian Ji, Zhangjie Qin, Zheng An, Bowen Yan, Daoheng Niu, Kunzhe Dai, Jingkai Fang, Dongyang Cao, Jiangyu Cui
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12938v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rydberg atom arrays natively encode the maximum-weight independent set (MWIS) problem through the blockade mechanism, so the Boolean circuit satisfiability problem (Circuit-SAT) can be brought onto the platform once it is reduced to MWIS. The conventional encoding of Circuit-SAT in the Rydberg atom array proceeds through conjunctive normal form (CNF) and incurs a substantial atom overhead. We introduce CAMERA (Circuit-SAT Atom-efficient MWIS Encoding for Rydberg Arrays), a method that provides MWIS encodings of Circuit-SAT instances on the king subgraph geometry of the array. CAMERA represents each logic gate as a compact weighted gadget and assembles the gadgets with a placement and routing compiler inspired by very large scale integration (VLSI) design. On random multi-gate benchmarks, the direct encoding route lowers the atom cost relative to the CNF route by an average factor of [MATH]. To demonstrate that the encoding extends from individual weighted gadgets to multi-gate arithmetic blocks, we compile a full adder and a multiplier, verifying each against its complete truth table by exact classical ground state calculations. We further showcase solving a representative Circuit-SAT instance end-to-end, from gate level compilation through a closed-system tensor-network simulation of a hardware-compatible annealing protocol on the encoded 30-atom instance to readout of a satisfying assignment. These results establish a complete encoding and simulation workflow as a proof of principle, and a concrete route toward solving a broader family of combinatorial problems on Rydberg atom arrays.
tldr: This paper introduces CAMERA, a method to efficiently encode Circuit-SAT problems into Rydberg atom arrays via MWIS, reducing atom overhead compared to CNF-based encodings.
motivation: Rydberg atom arrays can natively solve MWIS, but encoding Circuit-SAT via CNF is atom-inefficient. The authors aim to reduce the atom cost to make the platform more practical for combinatorial problems.
method: CAMERA represents each logic gate as a compact weighted gadget and uses a VLSI-inspired placement and routing compiler to assemble them on the king subgraph geometry. The encoding is verified via exact ground state calculations and tensor-network simulations.
result: The direct encoding reduces atom cost by an average factor compared to CNF, and they demonstrate compiling and verifying a full adder and multiplier, as well as end-to-end simulation of a 30-atom instance.
conclusion: This work establishes a complete encoding and simulation workflow for solving Circuit-SAT on Rydberg atom arrays, offering a concrete route toward broader combinatorial problem solving on this platform.

title: Geometry Versus Excitation Sector In The Decoherence Of Asymmetric $N$-qubit $w$ States
authors: Sougata Bhattacharyya, Sovik Roy, Fatih Ozaydin
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12965v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate how network geometry and excitation sector separately control pairwise entanglement decay in asymmetric multipartite [MATH] states. To disentangle these effects, we introduce an analytically tractable [MATH]-qubit generalization of the asymmetric Lohmayer geometry and its complementary-excitation partner, yielding inequivalent vertex-base (VB) and base-base (BB) pair classes that can be compared directly with symmetric [MATH]-state references. We derive closed-form concurrence dynamics under representative one-sided noise models and find that, within either excitation sector, the VB concurrence has exactly the same noise dependence as the corresponding symmetric reference, preserving a noise-independent proportional advantage wherever both remain entangled. The amplitude-damping reordering previously identified for the three-qubit Lohmayer state is therefore a cross-sector effect rather than an intrinsic fragility of the VB geometry. In contrast, the BB pair exhibits a genuine same-sector structural fragility, with lower entanglement-sudden-death thresholds than the VB pair under depolarizing noise and, in the [MATH]-excitation sector, under amplitude damping. The results establish network geometry, excitation sector, and noise symmetry as distinct ingredients governing pairwise entanglement robustness in asymmetric quantum networks.
tldr: This paper analyzes how network geometry and excitation sector independently affect pairwise entanglement decay in asymmetric N-qubit W states under noise.
motivation: To disentangle the effects of network geometry and excitation sector on entanglement robustness in asymmetric quantum networks, which is important for quantum communication.
method: Introduces an analytically tractable N-qubit generalization of the asymmetric Lohmayer geometry and its complementary-excitation partner, deriving closed-form concurrence dynamics under one-sided noise models.
result: Finds that within each excitation sector, vertex-base concurrence has the same noise dependence as symmetric references, while base-base pairs show genuine structural fragility with lower entanglement-sudden-death thresholds.
conclusion: Network geometry, excitation sector, and noise symmetry are distinct factors governing entanglement robustness, with implications for designing asymmetric quantum networks.

The authors introduce an analytically tractable N-qubit generalization of the asymmetric Lohmayer geometry, along with its complementary-excitation partner, to disentangle these effects. This construction yields two inequivalent pair classes—vertex-base (VB) and base-base (BB)—which are compared directly with symmetric W-state references. The study derives closed-form concurrence dynamics under representative one-sided noise models, including depolarizing and amplitude-damping noise. title: Pulse Engineering Of Quantum Many-Body Dynamics: Emergent Scar States, Entanglement, And Nonstabilizerness
authors: Prasant Mallik, Arkaprava Sil, Sudipto Singha Roy
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12559v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding and coherently controlling the properties of interacting quantum many-body systems is a central challenge in non-equilibrium quantum physics. While in the past decades, a wide range of many-body Hamiltonians have been introduced to study quantum chaos, atypical eigenstates, and quantum resources, systematically engineering and continuously tuning these properties within a single microscopic model remains largely unexplored. Here, we employ a pulse engineering scheme to construct an effective Hamiltonian that continuously interpolates between a chaotic Heisenberg (XXX) chain with a local impurity and the ZX Hamiltonian. Along this interpolation, we identify several families of analytically tractable atypical eigenstates embedded in the excited-state spectrum with distinct entanglement and nonstabilizerness properties. In the XXX limit, these states exhibit exact plateaus in both entanglement and stabilizer R\'enyi entropy and correspond to coherent superpositions of long-range valence-bond solid (VBS) states. As the pulse strength increases, the effective Hamiltonians exhibit a hierarchy of new set of approximate entanglement plateaus in the low-energy spectrum. Interestingly, in the fully pulse-engineered ZX limit, we uncover a distinct pair of long-range entangled stabilizer eigenstates, corresponding to rainbow scar states. We further show that pulse engineering preserves the distinct chaotic and non-chaotic regimes of the original model, while that is largely absent in the dynamical generation of entanglement and nonstabilizerness. The pulse-engineered models generate nearly identical quantum resources in both regimes, revealing a partial decoupling between quantum chaos and quantum-resource generation. Our results establish pulse engineering as a versatile framework for generating many-body Hamiltonians with structured eigenstates and tunable quantum resources.

motivation: The authors aim to systematically engineer and continuously tune quantum many-body properties like chaos, atypical eigenstates, and quantum resources within a single microscopic model, which has been largely unexplored.
method: They employ a pulse engineering scheme to build an effective Hamiltonian that interpolates between a chaotic Heisenberg chain with impurity and the ZX Hamiltonian, and analytically identify families of atypical eigenstates.
result: They find exact entanglement and stabilizer Rényi entropy plateaus in the XXX limit, approximate plateaus at intermediate pulse strengths, and rainbow scar states in the ZX limit. Pulse engineering preserves chaotic/non-chaotic regimes but generates similar quantum resources in both.
conclusion: Pulse engineering provides a versatile framework for generating many-body Hamiltonians with structured eigenstates and tunable quantum resources, and reveals a partial decoupling between quantum chaos and quantum-resource generation.

title: Intermediate Scattering Function Of Brownian Particles In A Tilted Cosine Potential
authors: Thomas Franosch Regina Rusch
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12421v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We solve the Fokker-Planck equation for a Brownian particle in a tilted cosine potential and derive the intermediate scattering function (ISF), which captures the full spatio-temporal dynamics of the system. The model consists of a single overdamped Brownian particle in one dimension. We derive a generalized ISF comprising two wave vectors to describe correlations in the periodic potential. Exploiting the periodicity via Bloch's theorem, we formulate the problem within a spectral-theoretical framework and numerically compute the corresponding eigenfunctions and eigenvalues, from which we obtain the ISF and the probability density. Using time-dependent perturbation theory, we expand the ISF and derive low-order moments, including the mean-square displacement, time-dependent diffusivity, skewness, and the non-Gaussian parameter. Our analytical results are validated by Brownian-dynamics simulations and analyzed focussing on different regimes of the tilting force. The results are compared to a harmonic approximation and the deterministic limit.
tldr: This paper solves the Fokker-Planck equation for a Brownian particle in a tilted cosine potential and derives the intermediate scattering function, focusing on classical stochastic dynamics.
motivation: The authors aim to provide a complete analytical and numerical description of the spatio-temporal correlations of a Brownian particle in a periodic potential, which is relevant to condensed matter and soft matter physics.
method: They use Bloch's theorem to exploit periodicity, formulate the problem in a spectral-theoretical framework, and compute eigenfunctions and eigenvalues numerically. They also apply time-dependent perturbation theory to derive low-order moments.
result: They obtain the intermediate scattering function, mean-square displacement, time-dependent diffusivity, skewness, and non-Gaussian parameter, validated by Brownian-dynamics simulations.
conclusion: The work provides a detailed characterization of the dynamics in a tilted periodic potential, but it is not connected to quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Dynamical Uncertainty Geometry For Nonlinear Transport
authors: Giacomo Tommei
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12521v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Uncertainty in nonlinear dynamical systems is often organized by transport structures that are not apparent from posterior geometry alone. We introduce Dynamical Uncertainty Geometry (DUG), a framework that separates three ingredients that are frequently conflated: posterior uncertainty, future observations, and model-induced transport. DUG indexes posterior credible sets and transport-conditioned subsets by a common enclosed-probability coordinate, allowing physically meaningful classes to be tracked across credibility levels rather than examined at a single threshold. The framework combines a mass-ranked credible filtration, a description of future experiments through their induced probability laws and Fisher geometry, and a labelled transport skeleton representing dynamically distinct outcomes. We establish stability results for the resulting mass-indexed persistence modules under simultaneous perturbations of posterior density and probability measure, including continuum, refinement, and finite atomic formulations. These results provide quantitative control of persistence computed from numerical approximations and weighted grids. Two benchmark problems illustrate the framework. In a short-arc orbit-determination setting, DUG identifies dynamically distinct return classes within a connected uncertainty region and highlights a difference between information-based and local Fisher-based observation-design criteria. In the Earth-Moon planar circular restricted three-body problem, DUG reveals multiple first-hit transport outcomes coexisting within a connected credible region and provides diagnostics for assessing their numerical resolution. Together, these examples show how topological summaries of posterior geometry, when coupled to transport labels and future experiments, yield a richer description of uncertainty than either posterior probabilities or dynamical classifications alone.
tldr: This paper introduces a framework for analyzing uncertainty in nonlinear dynamical systems using topological data analysis, but it is not related to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: The authors aim to separate posterior uncertainty, future observations, and model-induced transport in nonlinear dynamical systems, which are often conflated.
method: They propose Dynamical Uncertainty Geometry (DUG), combining mass-ranked credible filtrations, Fisher geometry of future experiments, and labelled transport skeletons, with stability results for persistence modules.
result: DUG is applied to orbit determination and the Earth-Moon three-body problem, revealing distinct transport outcomes within connected credible regions.
conclusion: The framework provides richer uncertainty descriptions by coupling topological summaries with transport labels and future experiments, but it is outside the user's research interests.

title: Ising-machine-like Driving Condition Restrictions In Ssbm And Additional Pseudo-annealing- Driving Method For Ssbm That Achieves Best Cut Value Search -
authors: Toshiya Sato
abstract: ArXiv:2608.12545v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In our previous paper, we described the proposal and validation of a new physical implementation-type simulator (spontaneous symmetry breaking machine (SSBM)) for a combinatorial optimization problem that utilizes a phenomenon dual to the model in which a pseudo-spin many-body system is created by spontaneous symmetry breaking. Furthermore, we performed numerical simulations with different initial fluctuations on a large-scale benchmark problem (K_{2000}) and reported that we identified a condition under which pseudo-spin patterns gradually converge during the solution search process to ultimately form a single pattern and that the cut value of this converged solution reached 99.7% of the known best.
